evals.prompt: Define the Kano model in 2-3 sentences. Include what it classifies and name at least four response categories.
expected_elements: Defines Kano as a customer-satisfaction / feature-classification model
Explains that it compares satisfaction when a feature is present versus absent
Names must-be or basic quality
Names performance or one-dimensional quality
Names attractive or delighter quality
Names indifferent, reverse, or questionable quality

evals.prompt: Explain the mental model of Kano analysis. Name the primitives and how they connect.
expected_elements: Names customer segment or persona
Names candidate feature or capability
Names functional and dysfunctional questions
Names satisfaction and dissatisfaction responses
Explains classification by response pattern
Explains that categories guide prioritization differently

evals.prompt: Why does a Kano-model skill exist for agents? Name the decision failures it prevents.
expected_elements: Prevents treating all requested features as equally valuable
Prevents ranking delighters before unmet basics
Prevents mistaking absence of complaints for satisfaction
Prevents using simple yes/no preference questions as Kano evidence
Prevents assuming one segment's category applies to every segment

evals.prompt: Distinguish Kano analysis from prioritization, user research, positioning, expected value, and methodology. Give a mechanism-level reason each neighbor is different.
expected_elements: Prioritization scores or ranks work across criteria
User research gathers and synthesizes customer evidence
Positioning chooses market context and differentiated value
Expected value compares probability-weighted outcomes
Methodology owns broad process design
Kano classifies customer satisfaction response patterns to feature presence and absence

evals.prompt: Place the Kano model among product strategy and research methods. What upstream inputs feed it, and what downstream outputs can follow it?
expected_elements: Classifies it as a customer-needs / product-prioritization / quality model
Names upstream inputs such as segment definition, feature hypotheses, interviews, surveys, or usage evidence
Names downstream outputs such as feature categories, must-be gaps, performance trade-offs, delighter candidates, or roadmap input
Explains it can feed but not replace ranking, sizing, and strategy decisions

evals.prompt: Give an analogy for the Kano model that preserves the different satisfaction curves. Then name one bad analogy and explain what it loses.
expected_elements: Uses an analogy involving different kinds of levers, controls, shelves, or signals
Maps must-be to preventing dissatisfaction
Maps performance to proportional satisfaction
Maps attractive to surprise upside
Rejects an analogy that treats all features as points on one linear score

evals.prompt: Novel scenario: A team says users ask for export CSV, dark mode, faster search, animated confetti, and fewer signup fields. Apply Kano reasoning by diagnosing what evidence is missing and how the categories might change the roadmap.
expected_elements: Does not classify the features from names alone
Requires segment-specific functional and dysfunctional evidence
Recognizes export CSV or fewer signup fields could be must-be for some segments
Recognizes faster search may be performance quality
Recognizes dark mode or confetti could be attractive, indifferent, or reverse depending on segment
Recommends fixing unmet basics before relying on delighters
